utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed. Your Honour, before I call the next witness, who is Ambassador Okun, there are two short matters which I would wish to place before the Court initially. The first relates to a ruling, if it be a ruling, by Your Honour on the 10th of October in respect of conduct of the trial vis-a-vis documentation. I've managed to obtain the transcript and perhaps if that could be put onto the screen at this time, to assist all parties. Your Honour can see it relates to the Pre-Trial Conference where I actually mentioned about transcripts. I've had highlighted Your Honour's suggestion, if I use the neutral word, saying from the Chamber's point of view, if a counsel intends to cross-examine on a document -- does the Court have that on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have an image but it's unreadable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's readable here for a change but we'll see if we can highlight it. Is that readable now, Your Honour? "Before I turn to the Defence, from the Chamber's point of view, if a counsel intends to cross-examine on a document, the Chamber would expect that counsel to have copies of that document ready for the Chamber, other counsel, and for the witness." And then Your Honour says, "Now, with that indication is there anything that you would wish to add, any member of the Defence team?" And Mr. Vasic, presumably acting on behalf of all parties, indicates quite clearly on behalf of all the Defence team, that that is exactly the view that they share. Yesterday - I make no criticism of it; it serves no purpose - the witness was cross-examined on a document. We did not have copies of that document provided by the Defence. Neither did the Court. All I am submitting at this stage is that Your Honour made a very specific reference to the procedure. We would submit in the common law jurisdiction and the civil law jurisdiction, that there should be equality of arms in relation to the production of documentation and that that was not done yesterday, and we would now, dealing with matters today and thereafter, seek an order that if such cross-examination is to be conducted by either party, that that party should provide to the other side copies of the documents so that the other side should not be disadvantaged unreasonably. That would be the first matter that I would seek an order on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is no need for an order, Mr. Moore; the order is already in place. You have referred to it. Could I add that as we are planning to conduct this trial so far as practicable on the E-Court system, that where documents are available and known to counsel in advance, they should be duly incorporated into the folder of their respective client in the E-Court system in advance so that when cross-examination on that document is undertaken, the document will be readily available. The resort to paper as a fallback is necessary at least at this stage of the trial because of the short notice. Hopefully, once we get past the Christmas break, that will have been overcome by all parties, but if it is that documents are to be used, copies should be available for all other parties and the Chamber. And with documents that are of particular significance, the Chamber would reiterate the value of those being available in paper form as well as in the electronic system, if they are in the electronic system, for the practical convenience at least of the Chamber, if not all other parties. Now, I don't think I need to reiterate. The order was there, the rules and the practice direction are there in those respects. That can be a little awkward with very large documents, to which only limited reference is made and that should involve discussion between counsel to see whether it's really necessary to reproduce the full extent of large documents rather than merely significant passages to which reference is being made. And we will certainly understand as a Chamber if counsel are able to agree that only parts of a large document are incorporated into the electronic system and made available in paper form.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is the first matter. May I deal with the second matter? It relates to the book that was referred to yesterday. I make no significant complaint about it. We did ask for copies from my learned friend, if they would perhaps provide a copy so we could photocopy it at the end of the day. That was refused. That's entirely perhaps the prerogative of the Defence. However, if that be the case, then I would seek an order from the Court for an independent party to seek to the doctor to obtain a copy of that book so that we have access to it. We ourselves, because of the court order, quite properly cannot speak to the witness. So we would merely ask leave of the Court for an independent party to speak to the doctor when he returns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, is there any reason why that book is not available? I turn to you, Mr. Borovic. You used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was waiting for the interpretation to finish, Your Honour. Your Honour, the book is in the possession of the Defence of Mr. Sljivancanin, the copy that I used. But I think it would be fair to my learned friend from the OTP to say this: We did not mean to use the book to manipulate. I tried to explain briefly yesterday, we had been given some information just before our cross-examination of the witness. We complained to the Chamber about our concern to not have sufficient time to tackle the new allegations by that witness. We had received the book but we had no time to even scan it for it to be possibly tendered into evidence. This is the procedure. We need at least 24 hours to hand our copy over to an officer who will then transfer it into the system. All in all, it is only a very small portion of the book that we quoted. It was just something we showed the witness in a bid to oppose the witness's new statement delivered as an addendum to the Defence teams 24 hours before the examination-in-chief. Therefore, to sum it up, I'm not the owner of this book and Mr. Moore has referred to the wrong person. The reason I have just indicated is why I was in no position to provide a copy. If you would be so kind, Your Honours, Mr. Lukic would like to add something in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I must return to what you said previously about the decision. This is what you said with regard to the first question stemming from my dialogue yesterday with Mr. Moore, so to speak, which also gave rise to his address to you today, as well as this additional explanation. At the 15th conference and also when we discussed the deadlines for delivering documents according to the rules of E-Court this was in reference to the pages that a party was going to use and tender into evidence, and not just sections of documents and statements which would not be tendered into evidence. My understanding of your decision is if somebody wants to cross-examine a witness about the circumstances of a document that they have no intention of tendering, they are not duty bound to show this to the Court or to the other party. If that understanding is correct, that would make our position quite clear. I understand now, I understand that position now. But let me speak about the other thing in relation to this book. Mr. Borovic received a copy of the book that we used for our preparation, that we marked and underlined our copy in order to prepare our Defence. We found out about the existence of the book from a statement given by Mr. Njavro to the OTP back in 1995 because at the end of the statement he says I wrote such and such a book called this or that. It's very difficult for me even now to remember that somebody in the OTP, perhaps not Mr. Moore and his team, but since 1995 that they would not have been able to obtain a book that a witness had told them about back in 1995 as having been written back in 1992. I frankly find that to be quite unbelievable. On the other hand this copy of the book contains certain notes that we wrote down in order to use during our cross-examination. It was certainly most inconvenient for me to hand this copy over to the Prosecutor. If the Court so wishes I will obtain another copy of the book and provide a clean, blank copy to the OTP and will then provide the OTP with a clean copy, although I did believe at the time that I had a full legal basis to do what I did. But now I understand that your position is in relation to all documents regardless of whether there is an intention to tender them into evidence or not. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So that it is clearly in the mind of all parties, as I recall it has been made clear in the past, if counsel intends to use a document in cross-examination, or examination, or re-examination of a witness, that document should, where practicable, be included in the electronic court system and, as a fallback, be available in paper form and, as we all see, for practical reasons, there are certain documents in which it's very prudent to have it available in paper as well as electronic form, for ease of use and ease of reading so that it's all documents that are to be used, not just those that are intended to be tendered into evidence. Mr. Lukic, you seem to have provided the answer to everybody's problems, as usual. You will be able, you indicate, to obtain a clean copy of the book, and so make it available. We would be grateful if you could do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best. It's a Croatian edition. It was never printed in Serbia. Therefore, I will have to use my sources and contacts to obtain a copy, but personally I believe that the OTP may find it much easier than I to obtain a copy of that book. However, I will do my best to live up to the Court's bidding as far as this is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber looks forward to being able to read the book in due course. Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we move on now, please, to call the next witness, who is Ambassador Okun. Might I respectfully request that the Court spans for one hour because Professor Okun has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We understand that there may be advantage for his health to have a break at no longer than hourly intervals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry that you've been kept waiting a time until we've concluded to previous witnesses. Would you be kind enough to read aloud the affirmation on the card that is offered to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would you please sit down. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Examined by Mr. Moore:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Herbert Stuart Okun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it's right to say that you're also known as Ambassador Okun; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may lead the following evidence, that in actual fact you have had what could be described as a long and distinguished career in international diplomacy; is that right? That you served as an officer in the United States foreign service from 1955 to 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the early 1960s, while serving in the US embassy in Moscow, that was during the Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962, you had responsibility for translating the letters from Chairman Kruschev to President Kennedy?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the -- in 1971, 72, is it right that you negotiated on -- with regard to the agreement on prevention of incidents at sea between the United States and the U.S.S.R., and that was the first military treaty signed by the U.S.A. And U.S.S.R. After World War II; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was signed at the summit meeting between president Nixon and Brezhnev and that was in Moscow in 1972?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, in May 1972.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 1973 to 1975 you were the political adviser to the NATO Commander-in-Chief in the Mediterranean, that you were stationed at Naples in Italy with the specific responsibility of observing the situation in the former Yugoslavia, and reporting on the developments in respect of Marshal Tito who unfortunately at that time was becoming rather old?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the late 1970s, is it also right to say that you were the deputy chairman of the United States delegation at the strategic arms limitation talks with the Soviet Union known as Salt II?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1980, you were then appointed to be the United States ambassador to what was formerly called East Germany and that was a post you held until 1983; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. I was US ambassador in Berlin to the German Democratic Republic at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. From 1985 until 1989, you were the United States deputy permanent representative and ambassador to the United Nations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 1991 to 1997, you served consecutively as special adviser and deputy to the personal envoy of the United Nations Secretary-General, working on issues related to Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Macedonia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 1991 until 1993 specifically, your focus was primarily Croatia and Bosnia, and from September 1992 until May 1993, you were deputy co-chairman of the international conference on former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then from 1993 until 1997, you were a mediator in respect of the dispute between Greece and Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1996 until 1997 you were the special adviser to the international commission on missing persons in the former Yugoslavia, and I think it's right to say, academically during the 1990s, you were also a visiting lecturer on international law at the Yale law school, and I believe at present you are the professorial lecturer you are in international relations, international law, and institutions at the school of advanced international studies of Johns Hopkins University; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I just deal with one or two small matters? I think the first time that you visited the former Yugoslavia was in 1957 as a tourist and in the middle of the 1970s as a political adviser, as I've already indicated to the NATO Commander-in-Chief in the Mediterranean. Can I deal then please with resolution 713 which was passed on September the 25th of 1991 at the United Nations? As a direct consequence of that were you approached by the then secretary -- well, actually the chief de cabinet of the Secretary-General to accompany Cyrus Vance?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, that resolution incidently was Security Council resolution 713.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you be kind enough, please, although I'm sure the Court know who -- will you tell the Court who Cyrus Vance was, please?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, Cyrus Vance was a distinguished, highly distinguished, American lawyer and public servant. He was secretary of the army and legal counsel to the department of Defence in the 1960s during the administration of President Johnson and from 1977 to 1980 during the administration of President Carter he was Secretary of State. After that, he returned to his law practice in New York and continued to undertake important private missions for a variety of public and private causes. I knew him well long before 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that the purpose of that mission was what I will describe as diplomatic and fact-finding and to make recommendations to the Security Council through the Secretary-General?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it's also right to say that the European Community at that time, in September of 1991 and before, had through their conference on Yugoslavia that they had a comprehensive solution or were obliged to try and obtain a comprehensive solution to the problems in Yugoslavia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. The purpose of the conference on Yugoslavia, chaired by Lord Carrington, the former British Foreign Secretary, was to try to reach an overall political settlement for the problems in then Yugoslavia, with the aid of the Yugoslav parties themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I may briefly deal with the first parts, I think it's right to say that you arrived initially in Belgrade on Saturday, the -- October the 12th, and I think you were with Mr. Vance, that on the 13th of October, you met President Milosevic, and you left again on the 18th of October and subsequently reported to the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. If I might I would add that we visited the entire country in that period, and met with all of the relevant leaders, or most of them, and not just Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it's rite to say that throughout your trips to Yugoslavia, you compiled what I will call diaries and that they were contemporaneously recorded by yourself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you place inside the diaries? Could you give the Court a general synopsis of --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. It is practice to keep records of the meetings that one has, not a requirement. Diaries are not meant -- I mean, professional diaries are not meant to be stenographic records. But I find it very useful to keep fairly detailed, close records, of our meetings, of meetings in which I participate. It was particularly important to me, and I thought useful, because we would see many people in one day, many days lasted 18 to 20 hours of constant work, and we would be in three or four cities and have half a dozen important meetings during the day. Well, with that many meetings it's very easy, unless you keep a written record at the time, to confuse or misremember what happens. So I kept the diaries for myself and, of course, for Mr. Vance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Again I'll deal with your next visit fairly briefly and then deal with the third visit perhaps more comprehensively. I think there was a second visit between November the 3rd and the 9th November exactly the same form at as before, visiting around the country and speaking to various individuals; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. I would simply add that the major focus was on events in Croatia because that was where the fighting was. There was no fighting in Yugoslavia -- no major fighting, I should say, in Yugoslavia at that point except in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation to the reporting to the Security Council, again if I reported in very shortened form would it be right to say that you came collectively to the decision that a peacekeeping process would be the way ahead? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Mr. Vance and I, very shortly I would say, really after the first visit and certainly after our second mission, reached the conclusion that a peacekeeping operation could be useful and would be useful, of course, with the agreement of the warring parties, and it was then, in November, important to check this with the warring parties themselves and that was the principal object of our mission in November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to deal then with the third, what I will call return to Yugoslavia, that related to the 16th of November until the 24th of November 1991. Again, is it right that you compiled a diary throughout that period?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was compiled contemporaneously when matters were fresh in your mind?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you indeed I would seek leave for you to refresh your memory from that document which I know is in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, there are various diaries there. Perhaps if you could find the one dated 16th of November to the 24th of November, please? While the ambassador is just checking that, can I just indicate to assist the Court and all parties, we have provided a small blue file which should have number 62 on it. There is an index and refers to the various pages on the diary. They tend to be more easily read than perhaps the electronic screen but it is already in E-Court and can be done that way for the assistance of all parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, can I just deal, please -- do you have your diary before you?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to turn initially to page -- it should be page -- it's -- what is the page number that starts your entry into Yugoslavia, please?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: The entry into Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. On this particular --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: On this mission?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: It begins on page 31.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I add, sir, the reason it -- the Yugoslav section begins on page 31 is the diary begins, page 1, where our meetings in New York with Secretary-General and the Security Council. And then en route to Yugoslavia, Mr. Vance and I and our team stopped in Amsterdam and -- to meet with the EC representatives, the European Community, as it was then called. So it was -- and I kept records of all those meetings so the Yugoslav part begins on page 31. The mission begins on page 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed. Can we deal, please, with your arrival on Sunday, the 17th of November, where you arrived in Belgrade? If I again deal with it in general terms, is it right that you had various meetings with the ICRC and the UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you in very general terms indicate to the Court, and it may be on page of your diary, if it assists,?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: We would routinely see the representatives of the International Committee of the Red Cross and the UN High Commissioner for Refugees as well as other humanitarian organisations, in order to keep ourselves as well informed as possible on the humanitarian situation in all of Yugoslavia but particularly in the combat zones of Croatia. By mid-November, more than 200.000 people had been displaced, IDPs is the technical jargon term, internally displaced persons. The number was rising rapidly. As I say it was over 700.000. Indeed by Christmas it was over half a million so it was natural for us to speak with the ICRC representatives as well as those from UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would it be right to say that you also received communication from other diplomatic parties about concerns expressed over Croatia in general?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Fighting in Croatia drew attention not just in Yugoslavia or in Europe but round the world. It was heavily reported in the press, front page news day after day. So there was no lack of general information about what was going on. In addition, many countries were deeply concerned with what was happening. The EC, as we've already mentioned, had a formal conference and was in charge of the diplomatic efforts to find a solution to the problem, and the EC had hundreds of monitors in the country, mostly in Croatia, almost exclusively in Croatia, but a few in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was a group called the European Community Monitoring Mission, ECMM. You'll see references to them in my diary notes. So the situation in Croatia was of high attention and urgency at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Vukovar at any time mentioned in those preliminary conversations or briefings?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed. Vukovar would be almost invariably mentioned because the siege of the city had been going on since August. It was, I think fair to say, along with the events in and around Dubrovnik, the siege -- the attack on Vukovar by the JNA received more prominent attention, publicly and privately, than any other single occurrence during the combat in Yugoslavia. So one heard and read about the attack on Vukovar in the press, from the humanitarian organisations, and also from concerned governments. For example, on our arrival in Belgrade, I think it was the 17th, the German ambassador called on Mr. Vance and me to convey to us the deep concern of Foreign Minister Genscher about the worsening situation in Vukovar. So that the overall problem Vukovar specifically the humanitarian situation, and what many people saw as a looming tragedy, was widely known. Indeed, the situation of the people in the besieged city was known. The ICRC rep and others referred to those who were underground in hiding, and hospital and other places, as "mushroom people." I noted that in my diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What reference do you have in your diary about that, please. Is it page 59?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Might I look for it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: No. It's not on page 59. Excuse me. If you give me a moment, I can find it. It's on page 39. Page 39, date Monday, 18 November, 1991, in a meeting with the representative of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, Ms. Cumin, and the representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross, Mr. Mira [phoen]. If I may read, it's only a few lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: I note in the diary on page 39, and I quote, "Heavy shelling at Osijek, four deaths a day. Mushroom people of Vukovar. Dubrovnik shelling heavy, now quiet." So Vukovar was -- the mushroom people were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we deal, then, please, with tab 1? It refers to top --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise for interrupting my learned friend, the Prosecutor, as he was cross-examining. There was a need to react, though. I believe the Defence is now facing the same sort of situation that my learned friend spoke about at the beginning of today's session. We heard the witness today talking about events that he personally witnessed and recorded in his diary. The Defence, however, has not been given copies of these entries. We find it extremely difficult to follow the witness's testimony as we are not able to follow what he actually wrote down in his diary. We did receive other pages of the diary from the OTP but not the ones in reference to the events that the witness is now being cross-examined on. We have no idea what is stated in those pages, and I start out with the assumption, of course, that the OTP is in possession of these pages. I believe it would be extremely useful for both the Defence and the Chamber to have these pages in front of us so that we may be better able to follow as the witness is testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We can get a copy very quickly from page 39. We thought it was at page 59, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If it helps, my papers commence at page 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, it does. And indeed all should commence at page 60 because that's the relevant date as such but we'll certainly get a copy of that. It can be done immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You say that it's on the E-Court system?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't believe the whole diary, because the diary document itself is an enormous document. It's two full files, and so one has tried to extract documents that relate merely to what I will call Vukovar because clearly Ambassador Okun's missions over a period of time related to a much broader spectrum much time and geographic location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So we haven't got page 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You wouldn't have page 39.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We look forward to receiving the paper form.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That can be done today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic for mentioning that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, could we be kind enough please to move to page 60 which I know all parties do have a copy of. Here we have got, I believe, the 18th of the 11th; is that right, in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you go to tab 1, which are photocopies of your original diary, you see page 60 and then page 61. We've got Belgrade 18th of the 11th, can you tell us, please, in very general terms what your entry on page 60 relates to, please?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: The entry on page 60 is the concluding page of the day in Belgrade. It was a busy day. It began in my diary on page 39. The rest isn't particularly relevant. It's meetings with Milosevic, Jovanovic, lengthy meeting with those two gentlemen. Lunch with Milosevic and Jovanovic. Then on to General Kadijevic, Admiral Borovac, Colonel Obradovic, long meeting, long meeting with General Kadijevic and his men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at page 60 --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: And page 60 concerns a meeting with the federal Prime Minister, Ante Markovic, which was the last meeting and therefore the last entry of the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If one looks at the bottom of page 60, there is reference to "general discussion of." Can you tell us please to what that relates?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. This it was a meeting, as I say, with Mr. Vance and I, along with meeting with Prime Minister Markovic and then an undersecretary from the Yugoslav foreign ministry, Mr. Veres, and it was not our first meeting with the Prime Minister. We had met with him several times before. And I note at the bottom of page 60, that, in addition to the specific subjects that we covered above, that we discussed the role of President Tudjman, that is to say how secure he was in his position, his attitudes towards the attacks on his country and people. That sort of thing. We had a general -- a discussion, an important one, of the rising extremism throughout Yugoslavia because that was evident to us, and of great worry to Mr. Vance and to me, and also to the Prime Minister. And we discussed Bosnia and Herzegovina, which, as you can see from the notes, Prime Minister Markovic referred to as an atom bomb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Can we then move, please, to November the 19th, page 61? It's a Tuesday. And clearly, there is reference to locations of places that you went, Belgrade, Sid, Vukovar, Belgrade, Grac [phoen], and Zagreb and leaving at 6.30 in the morning. Now, what was the purpose of your visits on that day, November the 19th?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Because we had heard so many disturbing reports about Vukovar, Mr. Vance and I thought that it would be useful for us to see with our own eyes what, in fact, was occurring there, and if possible take some action. So we decided to visit Vukovar and asked -- requested from Milosevic and General Kadijevic assistance in doing so, and they agreed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we just deal, please, with the reference to 8.45 at the very bottom of the page, departure, and then 10.00 a.m. Arrival Negoslavci? Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bottom of the page? Now, can you please remind us of what your entry is in respect of that meeting at Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. I should say by introduction, we were taken this entire trip we were in the hands of the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA. We went there in APCs, in armoured personnel carriers, and at 8.45 we left Sid which is in Serbia, and an hour and 15 minutes later arrived in Negoslavci, which is due south of Vukovar in Croatia, and I note, if I may just read the three lines, at Negoslavci, "half hour briefing by JNA colonel, the commander of the southern front."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you describe him, please?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you describe him?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: And then I describe him. I quote from the diary about this, the colonel, "militarily correct but hard."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you come to the conclusion that he was hard? What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Hard is a polite way of saying brutal, and I came to that conclusion by his manner, of his half hour manner, the briefing, the strutting, the attitude, highly belligerent, not towards us. His general military bearing, as I said was quite correct, but it was also quite clear that this was a hard man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm going to play now a video and I hope to freeze it. This video is part of your visit to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see the back of whom I expect will be admitted to be Colonel Mrksic. Is that Mr. Vance?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that relates to the visit to Negoslavci. We'll play on if we may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was happening at this time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Well, we arrived and we were led into Mrksic's headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: And here we are seated at the table, and on the left you see Mr. Vance, in the middle is the peacekeeping fellow and I. And we are discussing -- Mr. Vance, that is, is asking about the overall military situation, describing the ideas we had, he and I, for the possible peacekeeping operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: And that sort of thing. But the focus was on Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Because we were en route to Vukovar, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we turn the page, please, to page 62, which should be tab 2? We have a reference to 10.35 a.m., departure Negoslavci. If I may just move on in time for a moment, in APCs and then 11.00 a.m. to 1.00 p.m., Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to this part of the video, that was caught by television cameras and we have the transcript of what was said. It's only a very short transcript but it may assist all parties and the Defence have had it served on them. May I just hand that out at this stage? It's in hard copy, just for ease. As I say, I've got page 39 which I'll hand out in a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, if you could be kind enough, please, to look at the video screen? Have you got a copy of the transcript or not? Have you been given one? And what we are about to see is a short clip of the drive from the APCs and then a meeting that you have with Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we play that, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, does that correspond with what you saw at Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Those houses looked in rather better condition than the ones I saw. Ah, yes. This is a familiar sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who this is, please?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. On the extreme right, wearing the tan rain coat is Cyrus Vance. To his right is the interpreter, and then the very tall chap in military uniform with the mustache is Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the actual transcript flows from this particular time and I hope that the sound quality is good enough to correspond with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just deal, please, with your notes for this particular period? If we just deal with your first entry, please, at 11.00 a.m. to 1.00 p.m., what does your note say?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: It says, "Situation report," which I wrote in German, "Lagebericht," and I wrote "the JNA obstructs the visit, but Cyrus R. Vance retrieves the situation by firmness and patience and persistence."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "JNA obstructs visit," what gave rise to that entry?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: That was -- that was specifically about the behaviour of our escort officer, Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what way did he attempt to obstruct you?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Well, you saw part of it on the video that you just showed. You heard him say to Mr. Vance, "I can't do that. I can't take you to the hospital." You could see the look of anger and sternness on Cyrus Vance's face because he had said it several times already. They had more than one interchange. And it was self-evident that Sljivancanin was not telling the truth. We were already suspicious because he had so told several obvious falsehoods to us already. For example, he claimed that the small JNA barracks in the town, in Vukovar, had been shelled and that hundreds of shells a day had fallen on the barracks but we walked through that barracks. We saw it ourselves. And it was almost untouched. There was almost no damage whatsoever done to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just deal with your note on that, if I may? It's slightly out of sequence, but I do so.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If one looks down to the third subheading on your note on page 62, there seems to be a reference to "visit to JNA barracks." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough, please, to read out what your notes are in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. It gets a separate reference in my notes, and I write, "Visit to JNA barracks," underline it, and then I write, and I quote, "Object of attack, JNA says, was to free relatively small barracks. They troop us through." So we had the opportunity to see with our own -- with our own eyes the physical and other situation, the entire situation n the barracks, bearing in mind that we had been told that this was the reason for the attack, for the JNA's attack on Vukovar, that they had been attacked and we could see that there was no damage done to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the transcript that the court have, there is reference to Major Sljivancanin, referring to before the Yugoslav People's Army unit liberated Vukovar, some 400 to 500 mortar missiles were being launched on our barracks daily. That's on line 1415. Have you ever served in the army?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I have, in the infantry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And looking at the JNA barracks, what was the extent of the damage that had been occasioned to those barracks?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Well, as I said, it was almost totally undamaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I just then return to what you said about the obstruction by Major Sljivancanin? How would you describe the mood between Vance and Sljivancanin when they met?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: It started out polite. Mr. Cyrus Vance is a distinguished former Secretary of State. He was, of course, courteous. But it deteriorated quickly, as Sljivancanin very obviously was seeking to prevent, indeed insisting, that Mr. Vance not be allowed to see what he came to Vukovar to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there anything specifically that Sljivancanin did that demonstrated to you that particular approach or attitude by him?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, there was one striking moment when they were engaged in what was more than an animated discussion. It really was a shouting match. I have never in decades of close association with Cyrus Vance, seen him as angry as he was that day, and he started to walk in the direction of the hospital that we were trying to visit because it was visible. We could actually see the building or see what we were told was the building, which in fact was correct, and at that point, Sljivancanin raised his weapon, his rifle, and that was a very memorable moment. He pointed it at Mr. Vance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Sljivancanin pointed his rifle at Vance, what occurred as a result of that? Did Vance continue?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: No, he stopped. I don't think that he thought, nor did I, I must say, at the moment, that Sljivancanin would shoot Secretary Vance but he was brandishing this long weapon, and talking at the top of his lungs very, very -- shrieking at Mr. Vance, and so it was quite clear that he was -- he was serious.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just try and ascertain location as best you can? Please don't guess. We have a map which you need not see, perhaps, as it's not necessary, but there is what's called the Vuka River and there are three bridges that cross it. How close were you to the bridges at that time? Are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Well, of course, at the time I didn't know the name of the river. We knew that Vukovar was on the Drava but we could see the bridges and we could see beyond. We were standing in a square, a rather small square, in the middle of the city. We had disembarked, of course, from the APCs that we were travelling in and we were expecting to walk to the hospital, which as I say was pointed out to us. So this scene, this shouting match, occurred in the middle of a small square.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like, if I may, to deal with one other aspect of your entry before we take perhaps a short break. If we look at the second head or subheading on page 62, I think you've written in French in this time; is that right, meaning setting?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: I wrote mise en scene, yes, the setting. What the place looked like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is -- what was your impression at that time from what you had seen? Can you tell the Court?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, if you'll permit me to quote directly from the diaries, I write mise en scene, I underline it, and then I read, and I quote, "Do not see downtown but much of the town seen nonetheless. Almost every building, every structure, is destroyed or shattered by shell fire. A few destroyed tanks litter the streets. Destruction everywhere."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Closed quote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like you just now to look at a short video and see if it corresponds with your recollection and, indeed, entry in your diary. Would you please watch the monitor?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have informed us that you had seen much of the town nonetheless. How does that video represent the town as a whole?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: The video is accurate. It describes visually quite accurately the -- it was a horrific scene, with almost every structure in the city destroyed or shattered, and the video is accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are, if I may respectfully suggest, a gentleman of mature years and perhaps have seen other towns or cities that have been ravaged by bombs and war. Would that be right or not?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How does Vukovar compare with some of the cities that you have seen in your life?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: As respects Yugoslavia, it was the most thoroughly destroyed city that I saw, and I think it's fair to say that existed. I was in Dubrovnik, Osijek, Sarajevo, and nothing in those cities, even Sarajevo, compares to the destruction of Vukovar. Nothing. It's as light today. I was in Europe in 1949 as a student, fours years after the Second World War, when a great deal of cleanup work had been done, but there was, of course, destruction in the west. I didn't go to the east. And I saw nothing that compared to what I saw in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Berlin?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Berlin was pretty bad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then finally in respect of this part of your entry, there is a fourth head, "visit to reception centre." It is the -- actually the third specifically. Would you be kind enough, please, to indicate to the Court what you found there?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. We were taken to this reception centre, as I called it here. One could equally, accurately call it a refugee camp or a camp for displaced persons. But that's what it was. And I wrote as follows: "Visit to reception centre. Many affecting scenes of weeping civilians, reunited families, et cetera. Mr. Vance talks to the displaced persons. Many foreign press on scene. The centre is full of JNA and many rough customers, armed irregulars et al, and others. An air of brooding and imminent menace is conveyed by the Chetnik types."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you refer to phrases such as "brooding and imminent menace," when did you actually write those words? That day or days afterwards?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely that day because you could see the diary continues and at 7.00 I'm in Zagreb. It was written that day. It was probably written within the hour. On that trip and normally when we travelled, I would write my diary notes in the vehicle so they were usually written within oh, an hour, a couple of hours, of the actual event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then finally, there is a reference to "visit to small hospital." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough, please, to read that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. "A visit to small hospital. Mr. Vance is" -- that CRV is Cyrus Vance, "Cyrus Vance's request to visit the main hospital is rejected. Weak excuses by JNA. A scene ensues."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you refer to "weak excuse by JNA," to what are you referring?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: I'm referring here specifically again to Major Sljivancanin, whose name incidently I did not know at the time, but he was our he is court and was with us and I'm being rather diplomatic when I say weak excuse. I might easily have written "lies" by JNA because we were told obvious falsehoods. For example, Mr. Vance and I were told that the bridge across that river, the Vuka, I believe you called it, yes, the bridge across the river, which by the way is very small, it's more like a street across a stream, that it was mined and therefore dangerous and therefore we couldn't proceed to the hospital. We could see traffic on the bridge. So that was an obvious untruth. And we were told that, alternatively, alternately I should say, alternately we were told that the bridge had been destroyed. Now, mark you, this was told to us while we were within eyesight of the bridge. So there was -- it was a pretty clumsy and pretty obvious negative. I mean, in other words, it was immediate clear to us that no matter what you did, you weren't going to get to see that hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think it's right to say that we can see from the entry on page 62 of your diary that you depart Vukovar by armoured personnel carrier at 1.00 p.m.; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you had a fairly day thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll deal with briefly, but with the Court's leave I wonder if that might be an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the first break at this moment, Mr. Moore. The -- given the time, to allow the minimum time needed for the tapes, we will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, can we just perhaps move now to page 63 of your diary, top right-hand corner as we have it? I'll bypass certain parts if I may. I think it's right to say that between the hours of 7.20 p.m. and 11.15 p.m., you had a meeting with the Croatian President Tudjman; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, and his staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And his staff. In relation to that meeting, it's at page 63 of the original, do you have that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is it right that Mr. Vance indicated to President Tudjman that you had visited Vukovar that very day?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, he did, and I noted it in the diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you be kind enough, please, to tell the Court what was said in relation to Vukovar between Mr. Vance and Mr. Tudjman or President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Well, as I've noted in the diary on page 63, President Tudjman raised Vukovar and Kljuc and he said we are experiencing aggression, the Serbs are breaking the cease fires in Vukovar and Kljuc, and then he continued, Vance said, and here I quote from the diary, "We visited Vukovar earlier today. Tragic. Humanitarian problems serious. ICRC active, difficult task."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed. I needn't go into other matters. It may well be there will be some cross-examination in relation to that. You have mentioned that to President Tudjman. Would you be kind enough now then please to move to tab -- I think it's tab 4. It is page 97, top right-hand corner of your original document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it certainly seems to be 97 on the photocopy. 3.35 p.m. to 4.30 p.m., and I'm reading off the --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Well, I have on page 92, beginning on page 92, was our meeting which lasted a little less than an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but I think that's with another party. I'll come and deal with that in due course?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Excuse me, which page is it, then, sir, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. Could you please turn to page 97?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: 97, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed. The top of that page 3.35 p.m., 4.30 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I see it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed. I think it's right that you had a meeting at that time with whom?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: It is with Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was present at that time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: He had a notetaker with him and it was Mr. Vance and me, and our technical team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think it's right to say that you described it as a tete-a-tete, a one on one?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Well, for a few minutes before the general meeting, Vance and Milosevic spoke privately. I knew what Vance was going to say because we prepared these meetings very carefully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And would you be kind enough please to tell to the Court whether in actual fact Vukovar was actually mentioned?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, it was mentioned. It was the first thing that Vance talked about with Milosevic. If I might read from my notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: You see it in the middle of page 97 where it says CRV, Milo, that's, of course, Vance Milosevic. And I quote, "disagree strongly but politely about Vukovar. Vance, disproportionate violence, et cetera. Milosevic, Vukovar is a special case. The world will understand. Truth will out. The barracks were blocked, et cetera. Croats are brutes. One wore a necklace made of fingers of children. Now he's in jail, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Milosevic say what he meant by Vukovar being a special case?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: He did not expand on it, but it was so noticeable at the time, and this would have been written simultaneously, as he said it, that you'll note in the diary it's in quotation marks, meaning those were his exact words. We assumed at the time and we discussed it afterwards, Mr. Vance and I, between ourselves, that the word special case referred to something that either had happened or would happen which would be of a horrific nature but that somehow the world would understand it, but it was a noticeable remark, particularly coming from Milosevic, who was not given to that kind of statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough now, please, to turn back to divider 3? It relates to your pages 92 and 93, and refers chronologically to a meeting prior to the meeting with Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We see it's at 2.00 p.m. to 2.50 p.m., a meeting in Belgrade on the 21st of November. Who was that with, please?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: That meeting was at the Defence Ministry, with General Kadijevic, Admiral Brovet, General Jovic, and Colonel Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I deal then please with Mr. Vance's observations, of which you have made a note? Did he express any matters of concern in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, he did. If you note, and again this would have been written at the time, General Kadijevic at the bottom of page 92 says, and I quote, "Thank you for trying to help my country." End quote. "Your assessment is correct. You've pinpointed the problems." He was there referring to the discussion of the peacekeeping operation. And then General Kadijevic goes on to say, "garrison at Vukovar had been blockaded for two months before we moved in. Food had run out. People asked for the army's help." Vance uncharacteristically interrupted the general at this point because he was quite annoyed at hearing this same falsehood from the top of the JNA, so he interrupted General Kadijevic which as I say was quite unusual, and he went on to describe the obstruction of his Vukovar visit and I note that he did so "briefly but strongly."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whether you use the phrase "but strongly," when you're applying it to Mr. Vance, what does that represent?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Well, he was, of course, furious at the treatment he had received at the hands of Major Sljivancanin, particularly, and the JNA in general, in Vukovar. We've discussed the obstruction, the physical efforts to intimidate, the falsehoods that were told us, the demonstrative falsehoods that we had to endure. So, Vance in reporting this at his first meeting with General Kadijevic subsequent to the events was quite exercised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I want to deal with two aspects of this entry. If we look at page 92, in the middle of the page, we can see a reference to CRV, describes visit to the caserne. Can we just move down, please, to what had been given apparently a subheading of matters of concern? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the areas of concern described by Vance to these joint chiefs of staff?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: The first one I noted was the blocked garrisons and the reason it appears first was because, A, it was indeed a problem, and B, it was the principal item on General Kadijevic's agenda, that is to say the barricades of JNA barracks by the Croats. So naturally Vance would raise that first, and then he immediately raised Vukovar, the entry reads, "Increasing violence. Vukovar," and I write it in the diary it's written all in capital letters because he made such an emphasis on the point. Indeed he went in to talk about it at some length but I had no reason to write it all down because I knew what he said and I knew what he would say and I knew what I had seen. He described it about the way I've described it to you, Mr. Moore, this morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have actually in that entry actually words used by Mr. Vance in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Well, he certainly used the word, "Increasing violence.""disproportionate use of force" I put in quotes, so it means he used those words, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now you've told us that Kadijevic had referred to the blockade for two months. One of the parties who were present in this meeting was General Jovic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to assist the Court with regard to subsequent knowledge whether in actual fact that two-month period was accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: I think I can, because subsequent to this, indeed I think a year or so later or two, the former Serb member of the Yugoslav Presidency, Borisav Jovic, not the same Colonel Jovic -- General Jovic who is in this meeting but Borisav Jovic who was one of the leading members, if not the leading member along with Milosevic of the people's league of Serbia, that is the ruling Communist Party, and at this time in 1991, in the fall of 1991, Borisav Jovic was in fact the rotating president of the rump Presidency of Yugoslavia. Well, Mr. Jovic, this Mr. Jovic, later wrote a book about the collapse of the Yugoslav state, and I've seen it, and in it he says that the garrison at Vukovar had been relieved on September 20, 1991. Of course, we didn't know that at the time but it -- he certainly is in a position to know as the leading Serb president of the country, and if what he says is true, and there is no reason to disbelieve him, the shelling of the city continued for almost two months after the garrison -- excuse me, yes, after the JNA garrison had been freed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. I expect there will be some questions for you. Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Before my friend commences I think perhaps if he permits me I would make application for the documents that are compiled collectively in that small blue file as an exhibit. I'm quite happy for it to be done now. If there are any objections perhaps they can be aired now or indeed subsequently. But I would make application that the small bundle that I have prepared should go in the set as a single exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Vasic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. First of all, please allow me to introduce myself. I'm Miroslav Vasic, counsel for the accused Mile Mrksic. You testified in chief today that from October 1991 to May 1992, you were special adviser of Mr. Cyrus Vance, who was a personal envoy of the UN general secretary, is that the case?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could somebody make the translation come through a bit louder?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be attended to now. I think we will move on a little and you can indicate to the Court officer whether it's running too loudly or too quietly for you. Perhaps the Court officer could stay close at hand for a little while.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it all right now? While preparing for this mission that you took part in, I assume --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Now I hear nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now, sir?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. While preparing for this mission that you took part in, which lasted from October 1991 to May 1992, you must have familiarised yourself with the constitutional provision of the then SFRY as a federal state and the constitutional provisions of the -- of its constituent republics?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: I would not claim to be a constitutional specialist, but yes, in general, I knew the Yugoslav constitution, the one of 1974. I don't think I can fairly say that I remember very much about the previous constitutions. As you know there have been several.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer, sir. We are interested in that specific one from 1974 because it was still in force at the time -- period of time we are discussing now. Prior to your mission, you had worked as political adviser to the NATO commander for the Mediterranean, and you were involved in studying problems during Tito's time, problems with Tito's policies, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This new mission that you were assigned in 1991 must have appeared to you to be a much easier one since you were already familiar with the political circumstances as well as with some fundamental constitutional issues in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: On the contrary, it appeared to be a very difficult mission because there was a conflict going on, war was raging, people were being killed, and, as I've mentioned, there were already by October, November, that period, hundreds of thousands of displaced persons. It was by no means an easy mission, nor did we think it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Just before your mission, did you find yourself on another mission to Yugoslavia back in 1990?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what sort of mission and on behalf of which organisation?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: I visited Yugoslavia in 1990, December, with Mr. Vance and a team of financial and economic specialists. I was then, in addition to my other functions, the director of an organisation that indeed Mr. Vance and I had founded, along with some others, called the Financial Services Volunteer Corps. I repeat, the Financial Services Volunteer Corps. The purpose of this not-for-profit, private organisation, was to assist the former communist countries of Eastern Europe, all of whom had just come out from under Soviet domination at one level or another, and indeed to help the former Soviet Union after 1991, to help them in establishing market economies and free market financial institutions. Of course, they had none of that under the socialist system, so-called, in the Soviet Union or the former countries of the bloc. Nor did Yugoslavia have much of it under the system of worker self-management. So we visited Yugoslavia in 1990 to introduce ourselves, to let the leaders of the country know, and we visited all of them. We travelled from Slovenia to-- down to Montenegro and Macedonia, to let them know of our availability and that of the American financial community, to assist them in what was already evidently a difficult transition from the old command-oriented socialist system to that of the free market. In addition, in -- by December 1990, there were already indications that the political situation was becoming tenser. Indeed, while we were there in 1990, nationwide elections were held. So that was the purpose of our visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir for your explanation of this 1990 mission. In view of everything that you have just said -- can you hear me? I must tell you that the fundamental principles of the 1974 constitution, the SFRY constitution that was still in force in 1991, and at the time your mission took place, the fundamental principles of this constitution defined the right of all peoples to self-determination, including the right to secession.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: You're telling me that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, the people were granted this right. It's the people that were granted this right by the constitution, not the republics, which is only logical, if you consider the fact that Yugoslavia was a state composed of different republics, all enjoying different -- equal rights. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I am -- as I said earlier, I am not a specialist in Yugoslav constitutional law, so that I hear your assertions, I hear your statements, and my answer is I hear you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. All I wanted to know is whether this was something that you read at the time, these fundamental principles enshrined in the 1974 constitution. All I want to know is whether you're familiar with all of these. I'm not asking you to give an opinion. I just want to know whether you in fact read these at the time, the 1974 constitution more specifically?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware that the first sentence of it speaks of the right of the people or of the nations, as it is sometimes translated, "naroda" [phoen], into English, to self-determination and to secession. Yes, I know that is said in the constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the fact that following the multi-party elections in Croatia, which you said took place in Croatia in 1990, as you were touring the former Yugoslavia, and following specifically a HDZ victory in December of 1990, the constitution of the Republic of Croatia was in fact amended?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: I don't think I was aware of that at the time. Of course, we knew the results of the 1990 election. That was reported normally in the press.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you were preparing for the mission, did you never hear about the fact that the Serbian people living in Croatian territory were in fact concerned following these amendments to the constitution in December 1990, because they thereby ceased to be a constituent group in the Republic of Croatia and were to all practical intents transformed into a national minority?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: We were aware of that fact, yes, and also through the European Community, because, as we've already mentioned in previous questioning, from June or July 1991 on, the EC maintained active diplomacy with all of the Yugoslav parties and, of course, the situation in Croatia, in view of the fighting in Croatia, was known to the whole world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. In the context of my previous question, were you familiar with the concerns caused by the fact that the Cyrillic script, which up to that point had been the official script in the -- one of the two official scripts in the Republic of Croatia, was deprived of that status, although the Cyrillic script is the script used by most Serbs living in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. We were aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind the provisions of the 1974 constitution and its fundamental principles on the rights of the people to self-determination, bearing in mind the fact that the Republic of Croatia proclaimed independence unilaterally, do you not believe that this act amounted to a violation of the rights of Serbs in the Republic of Croatia, their right to self-determination?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Again, sir, I can only tell you that I can only state an opinion, not being a -- for two reasons. I should say three reasons I can only state an opinion. First because I'm not an expert on Yugoslav constitutional law at either the federal or the state level. Second, this issue is debated and very controversial and argued to this day by people who are specialists and experts on Yugoslav law at every level. And third, the European Community convened its own arbitration commission, the Commission d'Arbitration, under the chairmanship of Judge, now senator, Robert Badinter of France. That commission was composed exclusively of judges from the Supreme Court of various members of the EC, and they issued a number of opinions and decisions on these questions. So I'm prepared to accept what the experts say on this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the first conclusion of Badinter's commission? Did it not explicitly state that the SFRY continued to exist at this point in time, and that the republics failed yet to meet the requirements for independence? I'm talking about the very first finding of this commission.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: One would have to look to the subsequent findings because they will, of course, the subsequent ones naturally took precedence over the earlier ones, and I do recall one of the avis by the Badinter Commission. I believe it was in December, and I believe it was number 4, but that's just a recollection, in which it stated, in answer to the question posed to it by Lord Carrington, that the answer was that the Yugoslav state was in un processus de dissolution. The Yugoslav state was undergoing a process of dissolution. That was the avis. That was the decision of the Tribunal -- excuse me, of the arbitration commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In December. I fully agree with you. What I was asking is whether you're aware of their first decision dated September? If not, please state so. I will no longer be pursuing that matter.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: I may have been aware. I don't recall. In September I was not active on the Yugoslav case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that the constitutional court of the SFRY adopted a decision establishing the non-constitutionality of Croatia's decision to proclaim independence?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: That may have been mentioned in a conversation but I'm -- I can't recall it. I should mention, sir, that the political solution, if I may repeat what I told the gentleman earlier, the political solution to the Yugoslav problem was, at this time, in 1991 and 1992, the exclusive domain of the European Community. It was their job to deal with all these matters, and as I've also indicated, our job then, in concert with them, certainly we were in opposition, or competition, nothing like that, but Mr. Vance's job and mine was to explore the possibilities for a peacekeeping operation, which we recommended to the Security Council and then that was our task during this entire period until January 2, and then until February 21, 1992, when the Security Council passed Resolution 743 endorsing our recommendation that a peacekeeping operation be established in Croatia. So from October to February, and indeed afterwards, that was our focus, not constitutional questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
