utterances.text: By all means, sir. However, if this was to be a peace conference discussing the fact that one of the republics broke away from its state, it had to have some sort of constitutional foundation for these negotiations to ensure, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Lord Carrington worked very hard at that at the conference. I attended myself the meeting of the conference on Yugoslavia, of October 18, 1991, at which Lord Carrington put down the arrangements for a general settlement, the AGS, as the EC people referred to it, and these arrangements for a general settlement were a comprehensive solution to the problem of Yugoslavia, that problem it was encountering, and it included the kinds of rights that you are discussing, sir, namely the protection of the individual peoples, nationalities, minorities, however defined, and indeed there was a vote held on the Carrington proposal, the arrangements for a general settlement, with all of the Yugoslav republics present. The presidents of every Yugoslav republic were present that day in the conference, six of them. President Milosevic was there, Tudjman was there. They didn't vote but the others all did. The six republics voted on the Carrington proposal for a comprehensive settlement and five of the six republics voted in favour of it. One voted against. The five who voted in favour were Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Montenegro, and Macedonia. The republic that voted against was Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, and please correct me if I'm wrong, was this the October meeting at which the Yugoslav delegation walked out because --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... excuse me, I must correct that. Some walked out. In fact the Serb delegation walked out. It was the Serb delegation, plus Montenegro, yes. The rest of the conference, the rest of the participants, remained in the room. It was the Serbs who walked out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that Mr. Milosevic too was among those who walked out?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: No. As I said previously, he was not an active participant in the conference. He was there rather as an observer. But Kostic walked out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Kostic not there on behalf of the federal state, the SFRY and its Presidency?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: He was there on behalf of the rump Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the talks held in order to reach a solution to the Yugoslav crisis, there must have been discussion of unilateral decisions made by certain republics to break away from the federal state or to secede. Can you then please tell us whether Croatia at the time had one of the necessary attributes to meet the criteria for independence? And that is power, effective power, throughout its entire territory?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: I participated in no such talks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I won't ask any further questions, then, about that particular subject. Although you were still not special adviser at the time, but later on, when you talked to those who had been involved in these negotiations, did you ever hear that as early as in late 1990, the SFRY Presidency was informed by the secretariat for All People's Defence of the fact that paramilitary units were being set up in Croatian territory, in the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: We were aware after we began to visit the fighting areas that there were paramilitary units on both sides, that is Serb auxiliaries, paramilitaries, they were given various names, and also on the Croatian side. We were made aware by sort of normal conversation of the Croatians. The Serbs would tell us about the Croatians and the Croatians would tell us about the Serbs. So we usually received the information from the opposing party. That's not surprising.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the Presidency of the SFRY at one point in time in early 1991 passed a decision to disarm paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm sorry, but could the translation be made a bit louder? I've just got a lady's voice that I can barely hear. Can you raise the volume?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Is it better now? Can you hear it now better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now, Mr. Okun?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in early 1991, the Presidency of the SFRY adopted a decision to disarm paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Both General Kadijevic and Milosevic, I believe, yes, made that point to us. It would be somewhere in my diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in accordance with the 1974 constitution, the JNA, in the period of time that we are now dealing with, had a constitutional obligation to defend and protect sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity of the entire SFRY? Was it its main constitutional obligation?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Well, all armies are charged with the duty of defending their country against foreign - I repeat, foreign - invasion. That is invasion from without. In my own country, the United States of America, the army is expressly forbidden to act inside the country except with exceptional approval, and, if I may point out the importance that is attached to that, during the recent hurricane Katrina, the one that we all read about that flooded and buried New Orleans, the principal reason that the army didn't intervene earlier was precisely because the American army, like most democratic armies, is designed, its purpose is to fight foreign enemies, not to shoot at its own people. May I come back with your permission to your previous question, regarding the decision in 1991 to ban paramilitary units? I said that I was aware of it from Milosevic and General Kadijevic, but we have a saying in English, actions speak louder than words, and we saw with our own eyes Serb paramilitaries and auxiliaries on the ground, as I've reported to you earlier, and I so noted, we saw them in Vukovar at the reception centre, dominating and leering, passing the slivovitz from hand to hand with the refugees there. We saw them on other occasions as well. Later in that mission, in December, on a mission to Osijek, we went through Dalj which was the command headquarters for the JNA then attacking Osijek. This was December 1991. It's all in my diary. You may read it. And Arkan and his gang were there physically. We saw them. So I think -- I appreciate your recalling for my attention the fact that they -- somebody passed a law but it was clear to our eyes that it was not being observed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see paramilitary formations in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: You mean on the Croatian side? On the Croatian side. We saw them only at a distance but we were informed regularly of allegations that were made against Paraga and the HOS, the so-called party of rights. We knew very well that this was a neo-fascist outfit of the worst sort. Yes, we were aware. Our mission, sir, was to bring about peace between the parties. We went there with no animus towards either side. The record is clear in my diaries. We were always received, even at a moment's notice, by General Kadijevic, Admiral Brovet, by Milosevic, by Tudjman, Kucan, Izetbegovic, all the leaders were available to Mr. Vance because they knew that we were there at the behest of the United Nations Security Council and our task was to bring peace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have no doubt concerning that, Mr. Okun. Your mission had a successful conclusion ultimately but I believe that if you indeed wanted to achieve that successful outcome, prior to that you had to familiarise yourself with what preceded the conflict, how the conflict came about. This is why I put questions to you regarding the events which preceded your involvement in peaceful -- or peace negotiations. While you were active, while you were involved, did you receive information - were you told - about the attacks carried out by Croatian forces against the Serb population in Croatia in the spring and summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: General Kadijevic and Milosevic frequently alluded to that sort of behaviour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Kadijevic, the person you have mentioned, throughout the negotiations conducted there, did he ever express his concern and fears about numerous barracks that were blocked throughout Croatia by the members of Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. That concern, the blockaded barracks, was upper most in General Kadijevic's mind and we took it very seriously. We insisted with the Croatians that this stop, and I personally spent weeks going up and down the coast, in the Marshal Tito barracks in Zagreb, at the Zmaj factory, at the Zagreb airport. It was my task, Mr. Vance asked me, to take on the responsibility of ensuring, to the maximum possibility, that the Croatians stopped this activity of blocking the JNA barracks. We -- General Kadijevic took it very seriously and so did we.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I suggest that we take a break, and thus adhere to the schedule that has been pre-agreed, let me ask you something else. You mentioned that you visited the Marshal Tito barracks in Zagreb. If it's not too much trouble, would you be able to discuss to us the situation that was in place there at the barracks upon your arrival?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: I covered it very thoroughly in my diaries, which are available to you, precisely because we were so concerned with the situation of the JNA, and not just the soldiers, the officers, but their families as well, in the Tito barracks, as well as others. It is -- if I may, the report on the visit begins on page 82, Zagreb, November 20, 1991, and continues from page 82 through 85. So there are four pages. It's lengthy. I can summarise it for you briefly or I can read it all to you. It's a meeting we took with great seriousness. Shall I read some of it? Whatever you say. I'm at your disposal but it's all in the diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Okun. Since we have not received these pages of the diary, I would kindly ask you to give us the gist. Please describe to us in briefest terms, the feelings that dominated among the people in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we met with General Raseta plus eight of his officers, Vance and myself and General Raseta described quite strongly the situation, how they had been blockaded, that their apartments had been confiscated, and that the Croatian authorities were demanding that the caserne be evacuated, with the weapons left behind. Mr. Vance explained our mission to them, said in firmest terms that we believed that all of the garrisons should be unblocked and we're there to help. And then General Raseta continued and said that the JNA was being humiliated, that he himself had served in a UN peacekeeping force in 1963 and had very high opinion of the problems -- of the UN, a very high opinion of the UN. He said the situation should improve. Then he called upon General -- Colonel, Lieutenant Colonel Djurovski. Then Colonel Djurovski read us a prepared statement telling us about the barracks and giving us their view of the situation. He discussed threatening phone calls that were made, rude remarks, telephone lines had been cut. He said the caserne was fired upon, that they returned fire but small arms only. As you know, the Tito caserne is in downtown Zagreb. He stressed the ill treatment that he said the Croatian -- the families of the officers were receiving. And Mr. Vance, we asked them if they had reported this to the EC monitors, and Djurovski, Colonel Djurovski said yes, and then he told us he was born near Bitola in Macedonia, et cetera, et cetera. So we will a full discussion and indeed it was a very important one because we raised this with the Croatians and, as I said, Mr. Vance gave me the special charge which was a heavy charge, to ascertain, to make sure that the Croatians stopped blockading the JNA. Mr. Vance made it a condition for the erection of a peacekeeping operation, that is to say he told the Croatians that he would not recommend, that there was no possibility whatsoever that he would recommend a peacekeeping operation unless and until they freed the JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Okun. I'm about to propose the Trial Chamber to allow us to take a well-deserved break, if they find that this is an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now and resume at half past five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the break, we talked about how the barracks were blocked. Can you tell me, do you know what happened to the Bjelovar barracks after the members of the National Guards Corps entered the barracks? Were there any victims there? Casualties?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: No, I don't. I never heard anything about those barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was before you became involved in your mission. Tell me, please, in the basic document of Mr. Vance's plan, was there also an agreement to lift the siege of the barracks in the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: By all means. That was an essential component of the peacekeeping operation, as I've previously mentioned, we insisted upon it. And perhaps here, with your permission, I could describe very briefly the meeting of November 23, 1991, in Geneva at which this was agreed to by the parties. We brought them all to Geneva on November 23, Milosevic, Tudjman, General Kadijevic. We asked Lord Carrington to come to observe, Mr. Vance and I. We met at the UN's Palais des nations, and the result of that meeting was a public document that had four points. They were, first, a comprehensive general cease-fire. Second, the unblocking of the JNA barracks. Third, a commitment by the parties, that is the Serbs, the Croatians, and the JNA, a commitment to control their irregular forces, the paramilitaries, the auxiliaries. And fourth point, a promise to permit humanitarian assistance to go to the suffering people. That was signed in Geneva by Vance, Milosevic, Tudjman and Kadijevic. Of course, it was not observed in many respects and we had to take additional actions, but that was the fundamental -- one of the fundamental documents that we worked on. So the answer to the question was, again, on the unblocking of the barracks, was it a matter of concern, is not only yes but it was a matter of the highest concern to Mr. Vance and me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Okun. We will return to the issue of signing this agreement in Geneva somewhat later. Now I would like to turn to the negotiations that were led on the peaceful resolution of the crisis. Initially these negotiations were held under the auspices of the European Community, isn't that right? You yourself were not part of it initially.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: The negotiations for an overall peaceful settlement of the problem of Yugoslavia, the political-level negotiations, as I have mentioned, were the exclusive domain of the EC, and the period that it remained the exclusive domain of the EC was the summer of 1991, July, until August 1992, when, at a conference in London, the decision was made to merge the EC and the UN effort, and that led directly to the creation and the work of the international conference on the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned this period of time, summer of 1991 until August 1992, when the negotiations were organised or led by the European Community at the political level. Would you agree with me that during that period of time, they were not very successful in relation to these negotiations, not even when it came to the compliance with the cease-fire agreements?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. There was no question about that, that the EC effort was not successful, nor were their cease-fire demands ever met. I've already mentioned and don't need to repeat the Serb walkout, when Lord Carrington presented the arrangements for a general settlement on October the 18th, 1991, so it is correct to say that the EC effort failed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have heard, if I understood it well, that your observer role in these negotiations at one point in time changed and then you and Mr. Vance became active participants in the process, which led to the stage where Mr. Vance proposed a plan which solved the crisis in Croatia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. The plan -- what you call "the plan" we call the "peacekeeping operation." I don't mean to correct you, and forgive me, but people often to this day speak of the "Vance peacekeeping plan" and it was not that. It was routinely referred to by all the parties as a peace plan but it was not. It was in fact the peacekeeping operation based on the Geneva agreement that I've talked about and the implementing agreement which we signed with the parties on January 2, 1992. Yes. We -- that, as I've mentioned earlier, that was our principal purpose beginning in early November, to work out the peacekeeping operation with the consent of the parties and, of course, the JNA. The JNA was perhaps the most important party. That was our sole purpose and that's what is often referred to as the Vance plan for Croatia. It was in fact the peacekeeping operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanation, Mr. Okun. Did General Kadijevic present to you his claim that actually during the first stage of negotiations, when this was still conducted by the European Community, those who were -- conducted negotiations were precisely those who had initiated this crisis, aiming to see the dissolution of Yugoslavia, led by Germany among others? Did Mr. Kadijevic ever tell you about this concern of his?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, he did so frequently, as did Milosevic and others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these doubts and concerns, in fact, bring about a more active role of the United Nations and yourself and Mr. Vance in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: I don't think you can say, even now in retrospect, that it was just that issue. We were concerned about the fighting in general. Of course, we were aware of these concerns expressed by the Serb side, the political level, the military level. It was our job to find out what was on their minds. You can't devise a peace until you know the root causes of a conflict and above all, what the parties to the conflict are all about. So it was certainly something that was in our minds but I wouldn't call it the primary cause of the mission. The cause of the mission was the fighting itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vance and you were special envoys of the UN Secretary-General at the time. However, if I'm not mistaken, both of you came from the ranks of American diplomats. Can you please tell me what was the position of the American administration, in view of the Yugoslav crisis, in the summer of 1991, if you know that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: The American position had several parts. First, there was this same deep concern that the European countries had expressed, that the world was expressing but, of course, particularly Europe because they were the neighbours of Yugoslavia. Second, Yugoslavia was or had been for a long time a friend of the United States. The United States provided a great deal of economic assistance, weapons, trained JNA officers in American training camps for the military. Indeed, General Kadijevic told us that he had received training at the officers' training school in Arkansas in the United States. So there was a good relationship between General Kadijevic and Mr. Vance and me and all of the other officers, I may say, General Raseta, others. We had very good relations. In the summer of 1991, the American government at the time expressed its concern. You will recall that secretary baker visited Yugoslavia and Belgrade in early July, I believe it was, and at that time one was looking back at the history of Yugoslavia. All of us had been concerned particularly during the Soviet period for the independence of Yugoslavia. We were concerned about its territorial integrity, which was, as you know, under serious threat after Joseph Stalin evicted Yugoslavia and Tito from the Kominform in 1948. I don't need to tell you your own history. You remember it although it's long in the past. But beginning with that period, and even earlier, when American soldiers fought together -- fought with the partisans in the mountains of Bosnia and Slovenia during the war against the Germans and the Italians. So our relations were good and went back a long way. So that when Secretary Baker visited Yugoslavia, at the beginning of July 1991, he made all of this clear and expressed the hope and, of course, it could be no more than a hope, that the country would solve its problems peacefully, and remain together in some form. But the United States was not an active participant in the EC negotiation, and I think it's fair to say that Mr. Vance and I were the only ones on the scene aside from our normal diplomatic representation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. One thing I would like to ask you: You mentioned Mr. Baker's visit, the U.S.A. Secretary at the time. Do you know whether perhaps during his visit he ever clearly stated that the United States were in favour of the territorial integrity of the SFRY - at that point in time I'm talking about July 1991 - and that the US in fact would not recognise any attempts at unilateral secession by any of the Yugoslav republics? Do you know if he stated that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: No, I don't. I wasn't involved at all at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: I was made aware of that later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Okun, could we agree that all the way until the end of 1991, the Republic of Croatia had not yet gained recognition as an independent state and the SFRY continued to exist?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: I don't agree completely with your premise, Mr. Vasic. While it is true, the first part of what you said, that Croatia had not yet been recognised by the end of 1991, but already the SFRY, as I mentioned earlier, had been declared by the Badinter arbitration commission to be in a process of dissolution. On that basis I would say that the conclusion you would have to draw was that the state did not exist, that it was, in fact, in a process of dissolution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified in chief today about the 19th of November and you and Mr. Vance going to Vukovar. Prior to your arrival in Vukovar you mentioned passing through Sid. Can you please tell us, did you see if this town had been shelled at the time you were passing through?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: I refer you to page 61 of my diary notes because I've written that down explicitly, if I might read it to you, sir, to answer your question. I note that we at 6.30 a.m. we depart Belgrade in a JNA motorcade. At 7.45, one hour and 15 minutes later we arrive at Sid and stay there for one hour. And then I report on the situation in Sid. And I write, in German situation report, Lagebericht, "Sid is a large agro-business centre, untouched except for a few shell-pocketed buildings and a kindergarten shelled on November 5."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, do you know, if Sid is in fact in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I know that. I stated that earlier in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Were you told anything when you were in Sid about a wave of refugees from the Vukovar area, and do you know which ethnic group those refugees belonged to?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. We were informed about displaced persons. It's the second item on my report on Sid. I read it to you, "Mayor, youngish" meaning a rather young man, not like me, more like you, "gives us a briefing." I'm quoting, "Calls the Croats Ustasha. Refers to refugee in-flow from the fighting zones." I assume he was talking about Serbs. I'm almost certain that would be the case, Sid being very near the border between Croatia and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Are you familiar with the role played by Goran Hadzic at the time when you were involved in negotiations for a peaceful solution to the conflict in Yugoslavia or more specifically Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. We personally met Hadzic, and I'm familiar with his overall role in this period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at one point in time learn that Mr. Hadzic was in control of 95 per cent of all members of the Territorial Defence for East Slavonia, Baranja and Srem, meaning that 95 per cent of volunteers were under his control throughout that territory?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: To be certain in answering you accurately I would have to check my diary because I know I noted it down but my recollection is that Mr. Milosevic made that point to us, that Hadzic and what Milosevic referred to as the SAO of Srem Baranja, well, you know the geography, that Hadzic controlled the Territorial Defence. There was always an argument as to the status of the Territorial Defence because some maintained they were disciplined, others they were undisciplined, some said they were irregulars, others said they were auxiliaries. Many terms were used to describe them. As I said we saw them in action at the refugee centre in Vukovar. We met them again, Arkan and his men, in Dalj, outside of Osijek, in December, just days later than this. So there was a general awareness of the irregular forces, and if I might recall, the third point 3, the third item of the November 23, 1991 agreement on the peace operation, first our point was cessation of hostilities, second was unblocking the barracks. The third item was for all the parties to do their best, use their influence to bring the irregulars under control. So that was -- that was widely known. There were many references to it and, of course, irregulars were active on both sides of the conflict. There was no doubt of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please just tell me this? In order to have the agreement implemented, the agreement that you have just spoken about, did that require the approval of Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: I don't know that you could say it required his formal approval but it surely required that he take some action with his irregulars or with the TO, whichever you call or both. We raised the subject frequently with Mr. Milosevic, more than once. He told us to see Hadzic. We saw Hadzic. So that I think it is fair to say that Hadzic was certainly part of the problem. Whether he was part of the solution was in the hands of Mr. Milosevic, and you will find in the diaries very clear discussions between us and Milosevic on the need for him, that is to say Milosevic, to bring Hadzic under control because he was under Milosevic's control, and Milosevic assured us that he would do so. He promised Mr. Vance that he would take action with Hadzic and make him behave in a more correct fashion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to talk again about your visit to Vukovar on the 19th. I suppose you passed the JNA barracks on the way. Prior to your arrival there, did you know that the barracks had been under siege since the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: We had been informed --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want to know is since when the barracks had been under siege.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: We were told that the barracks had been besieged since August, I believe, perhaps earlier but certainly since August, and as we've already reported and seen and heard on the tape, we heard Major Sljivancanin allege that 400 to 500 shells a day had fallen on the barracks, and we visited those barracks at the request of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've heard that. Thank you. What I want to know is: Were you familiar with the fact that the commissioner of the town of Vukovar had ordered for the electricity, water -- and water supply to the barracks as well as the telephone lines, to be cut off in order to make their lives impossible? Is this something that you were familiar with?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: I don't recall whether that was ever mentioned, but we were in general, as I say, aware that the Croatians were taking that kind of action. We saw it and heard it at the Marshal Tito caserne in Zagreb. So I can say in a general way we were aware that part of the blockade of the barracks was frequently cutting electricity and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that during the armed clashes in Vukovar, there were several thousands of armed ZNG members and MUP members in the town of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: I don't think we knew the composition specifically of the contending forces. We knew there were Croatians in the city, Serbs in the city, civilians. We knew there were irregulars and probably some regulars in the city, and we knew that the JNA was shelling the city, obviously. We've seen the destruction. And we could see the gunners as we drove in. We -- of course, we visited the city on the day after it fell to the JNA, as they said to the day they "liberated" the city, and their gunners, the artillery men were still in the field, they weren't firing on November 19, but we could see the JNA boys and their guns. So we were, I think, aware of the violence that was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if I understand you correctly, you were not familiar with the specific numbers of the ZNG and MUP in Vukovar offering armed resistance, were you?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: As to specific numbers, no. I don't know that at that time it was possible to know, although I'm not claiming that as a -- any kind of an excuse. The fact that there was resistance, of course, was self-evident. Otherwise the JNA would have taken the city much earlier so it was self-evident that there was some resistance from the Croatian side. Of course, they were much the weaker side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In answer to a question by my learned friend, you showed surprise at one point, at one point during your stay in Vukovar. You were passing the barracks and you said that you were surprised that it had not sustained greater damage, and yet this surprise which today appears to be an important part of your impressions at the time, was not recorded in your diaries, was it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Well, when I wrote the diaries, of course, I'm not a stenographic notetaker, and also the diaries were basically who said what to whom and what we saw, but it was very clear, sometimes I mentioned it, sometimes I didn't. In Sid, for example, I noted that the town was practically untouched. I might have noted it. On the other hand, you know, that was a very busy day, November 19, and it began at 5.00 a.m. in the morning and ended at almost midnight, and I wrote down on the spot, you know, the things that I thought were most important, and sometimes I would just note where I was, you know, in the barracks case, they took us through the barracks, you know, that sort of thing, because I know very well what I saw. One can't forget that sort of thing. It's easy to forget words but you know what you've seen. I mean, you ask me to describe this room, in a general way I can tell you what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You also spoke about the objectives of the JNA in Vukovar. You confirmed today that you were aware of attacks that had been launched against the Serbian population earlier on in 1991, the summer of 1991. You were aware of the sort of situation that prevailed. What do you think would have happened to the Serb inhabitants of Vukovar, specifically had the JNA decided to withdraw from Vukovar, in which case the only forces remaining there on the ground would have been the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to that question. It's pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you proceeding on the assumption that Mr. -- that the ambassador has some particular knowledge of this matter, Mr. Vasic? Or are you asking him to theorise?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I fully accept what my learned friend has just stated. I do have to offer one clarification, though. The Defence believes that Mr. Okun was involved in these peace negotiations. He had information from both the Croat side and the Serb side as well as the federal state and the JNA. It struck me that perhaps at one point he may have been in a position to obtain such information that could show us whether the objective of the armed fighting in Vukovar was merely to lift the blockade of the barracks or to protect all the citizens from an aggression by the Croatian armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, the particular question you did formulate, and to which objection is made, I must agree with Mr. Moore that it's entirely speculative.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I will try to rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any information during your mission to indicate that members of the ZNG had been launching attacks against the Serbian population of the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: We were of course aware of the violence in and around Vukovar and other areas in Croatia. Western Slavonia, for example. We knew of, in a general way, of the events at Borovo Selo. We knew of the violence and certainly both sides were perpetrating acts of violence. But the fact was that the overwhelming use of force came from the JNA, and the preponderance of the violence came from the JNA, not from the irregulars on either side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your belief or do you know whether the Croatian forces were a regular, legal forces, based on the letter of law and constitution, or were these forces quite the opposite, illegal, military or even paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: They were of both nature. There was a constituted army of the Republic of Croatia. It had at its chief General Anton Tus whom I met and knew. He had formerly been the chief of the air staff of the JNA, one of the top JNA officers before he departed for his home country. So there was a regular Croatian army. And as I have already said in answer to previous questions, we were also aware that there were Croatian irregulars and paramilitaries, men like Paraga. Yes, we were aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer, Mr. Okun, but we are facing a situation with difficult legal questions to answer. We have the Republic of Croatia, which is legally not an independent state at this time. We have a situation where it cannot be allowed to have any armed forces proper. It can only be allowed to have TO forces. We are facing a fact that the National Guards Corps has been established but this cannot be based on any of the existing laws at the time because only an independent state can in fact establish its own armed forces. Wouldn't that seem to be the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I disagree -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to that question in any event. This is a matter of constitutional law. If the matter is going to be clarified, it would have to be clarified by a person who is qualified within that particular area, and in my submission, it is beyond the scope, with respect, of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I suspect that the witness would agree with you, but in terms of general understanding and impression, which is all that the Chamber would understand that the witness is addressing, I think this is a question which may properly be put. I would indicate to Mr. Vasic that the more you persist in the details of the precise constitutional legal position, the more you're getting away from general, public understandings, and getting into the field of expert opinion so that while the Chamber would allow this question on this occasion, you will understand we receive the answer well-conscious with respect that the witness does not purport to be an expert in this field or on this topic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I answer? No, I don't agree with your presumption. If I think of the history of my own country, its fight for independence, from 1776 to 1783, the United States had an army and according to what you've said, it would be illegal. I don't consider it illegal. General George Washington is a name perhaps known to you. I think almost every country that has had to fight for its independence has an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what about Mr. Kadijevic? Did he not at one of the meetings with Mr. Vance state, as far as the document signed in Geneva was concerned, that he was only able to take over command responsibility over the JNA but certainly no political role, that this was up to the Presidency of the SFRY and that the JNA would abide by any decisions plead by the presidency? Do you remember perhaps something to that effect being said?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes. He frequently said, more than once, that he was a servant of the state, that the JNA would always act within its area of competence, that sort of thing. He would make that statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. When he signed the agreement in Geneva, did he perhaps also qualify it by saying he was signing only the parts of the agreement that pertained to the JNA and its duties?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: I don't recall he said that. In fact, all four points of the Geneva agreement of November 23, 1991, came within the area of competence, at one point or another, of the JNA. To repeat: The cease-fire; the unblocking of the barracks; the control of the paramilitaries and the word used was influence, so it wasn't necessarily direct control. We knew that the chain of command was sometimes loose and informal. And the fourth point, the permission for humanitarian aid to go through the lines. So all four of those points came within the competence of the JNA, and General Kadijevic knew that surely. There was no argument about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I am mistaken in my conclusion that in November 1991, the decisive and dominant role, when it comes to the implementation of this item 3, was the role that the commanders and representatives of the TO Staffs had, as well as other commanders in that area and political leaders in that area called Baranja, Western Srem, and Slavonia. We touched upon this when we mentioned their leader, Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Well, they certainly played a role but we were always of the view, and we could see at the time the intimate relationship between the JNA and the Serb irregulars in the field. As I've already testified, and it's noted clearly in my diary, that at the refugee reception centre in Vukovar, there were JNA soldiers and intermingled with them, lounging about, passing the slivovitz from hand to hand were the irregulars and some TO. We had the impression, and very clearly the impression, that the JNA could basically do what it wanted with the irregulars. To start with, they supplied them with the weapons. And these people didn't have arms factories, and they had to get their weapons from somewhere. And they got them from the JNA. There was no secret about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you agree that at one point in time, both sides were armed, meaning the Croatian and the Serbian side, and that further arming was not needed because they had already had armed formations that they had command over in their local territory?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Part of that is accurate, and part in my opinion is not accurate. It's true that both sides, to a certain degree, were armed. Of course, the JNA being an army, serious army was more heavily armed than anyone, particularly in 1991. That both sides had small arms and that sort of thing, rifles, pistols, the occasional grenade, of course, was true, but in terms of the armament and in terms of the violence, in terms of the damage done, it belonged overwhelmingly to the JNA and we so reported to the Security Council at the time. So I am not speculating now 14 years later. I can give you the citation of Mr. Vance's report at the time, concerning the J -- the violence wrought by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The agreement that was signed in Geneva was signed by Mr. Vance as well?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. I didn't make a pause. Was this agreement also signed by Lord Carrington?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: I don't recall whether Carrington signed it. He might have. Certainly, Mr. Vance, Milosevic, Tudjman, and General Kadijevic signed it. Carrington was present at the meeting, at Mr. Vance's invitation. The document is a public document. One could find that out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't wish to challenge that, but it seems to me that Mr. Carrington left before the agreement was signed, and I wanted to know whether you knew the reason for that. Now you just told us that he was not involved in the implementation and the signing of this agreement, if I understood you well.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: Let me clarify it for you, if I may. The meeting of November 23, 1991, in Geneva, at the Palace of Nations of the United Nations, was a UN meeting convened by Mr. Vance in his capacity as the special representative. He invited General Kadijevic, Milosevic, Tudjman, there for the purposes that we have discussed. As I said earlier, he invited, as a courtesy, Lord Carrington, as an observer, and that was what it was. It was a courtesy. If you now tell me, or recall for me, that Lord Carrington left early, I would not find that surprising in the least. The day was Saturday, in fact. There was no reason for him to hang around once the agreement had been reached, and I think he -- I'm sure he shook everybody's hand quite politely and said good buy to them. He knew he was going to see them all in a few days in his capacity as chairman of the political conference on Yugoslavia. So I don't find it at all unusual that, as you now tell us, Lord Carrington departed somewhat earlier than we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that you have clarified his role, it doesn't seem so unusual to me either, as it did at first glance. After the unblocking of barracks, did the JNA forces withdraw from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: That's a long story. The short answer is yes, but it took a very long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I understood that.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN
utterances.text: It took until -- in fact, until October 1992. The implementing accord for the Geneva agreement concerning the unblocking and the total withdrawal of the JNA from Croatia was signed on January 2, 1992. The JNA left finally from Prevlaka in October 1992. So they did withdraw, one has to say, at a very leisurely pace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are aware of the problems with Prevlaka. Thank you very much, Mr. Okun.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much, Mr. Vasic. Because, Mrs. Tapuskovic, we've been limiting our sessions to about an hour, we have just had an hour, and it would seem that we would need to have a break now. That would leave us less than ten minutes after the break. I think it might be the more practical course, unless there is something you feel that you would very much like to ask in the next five minutes, the more practical course for you might be to continue tomorrow rather than this evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. If you have decided to take a break now, and this was a prior arrangement, to make breaks every hour, then I would gladly avail myself of this opportunity you just presented to me to begin the examination of the witness tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Tapuskovic. Given the hour and the circumstances, it would seem the most practical use of time would be to adjourn now rather than break for 20 minutes and then resume for a few minutes until seven. So an earlier evening, ambassador, than you were describing in your tours and work. But we will resume tomorrow at 2.15.
